content:
Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that despite Apple's claims that it reviews submissions, blatant rating manipulation on the App Store still goes unnoticed.

He says he doesn't intentionally search for scam apps on the App Store, but he frequently encounters them by accident, and shared a recent example…

The App Store is a 'safe and trusted place'

Apple takes a hard line against any antitrust measures involving third-party app stores or iPhone sideloading, often only backing down when legally compelled. Even so, Apple continues to defend itself.

The company claims it does this not for money, but to protect iPhone users from malware. For example, Apple said last year that it had blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, many developers question the claim that the App Store is a safe place, and point to multiple scams involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers who claimed their Bitcoin was completely stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store rating manipulation

App Store rating manipulation is a long-standing problem, with some companies even renting 'iPhone farms' in mainland China to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for his StopTheMadness Safari extension) points out that he considers the latest case of App Store review manipulation to be 'large-scale and obvious.' The app involved is TabControl Extension.

He says when he stumbled upon the app, it was ranked 12th on the US Mac App Store paid Safari extensions chart, and the screenshots displayed were obviously AI-generated fake images.

Another thing worth noting is that the fake screenshot claimed the app had a '4.9 out of 5' rating, misleading people into thinking these were App Store user ratings… Using App Store screenshots to make false claims is a common scam tactic, which I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself, but also App Store listing materials and metadata, including screenshots. The claims in scam app screenshots are often absurd to the extreme, but Apple routinely approves them anyway… Apple claims the App Store can protect users from dishonest developers. If App Store review can't even detect this kind of problem, then what's the point of review? In fact, App Store review doesn't need to investigate as deeply as I do. A screenshot claiming a '4.9 out of 5' rating is itself a red flag. Apple has records of all ratings and reviews for every country, so they fully know this is false advertising. I don't even need to download this damn app to know the developer is trying to scam users.

As he says, if a developer is willing to use deceptive tactics to promote their app from the start, you certainly wouldn't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's take

Of course, it's impossible to completely eliminate all App Store scams, but fake reviews are extremely common, and cases like this one should be obvious to Apple. What's puzzling is how this extension managed to pass review in the first place.

Apple should at least establish a mechanism to automatically conduct stricter reviews of any app that makes it onto the charts, checking both the app itself and the claims it makes.
